stories.headline: India rejects Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission ‘which is without any legal basis’
stories.deck: The MEA says there is no boundary between Pakistan and China; adds that J&K and Ladakh "are and will always remain integral and inalienable parts of India"
stories.bodyText:
India on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) rejected the "so-called" boundary joint commission set up by Pakistan and China, saying that the body has no legal basis to decide on arrangements related to Indian territory under illegal occupation.
New Delhi's reaction came following the first meeting of the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission in Islamabad.
India has been consistently maintaining that Pakistan's handing over of certain territories such as Shaksgam Valley to China in 1963 was illegal and unacceptable.
New Delhi has also opposed the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor as part of it passes through Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK). "Our position on this matter is clear and consistent. There is no boundary between Pakistan and China. We reject the so-called Joint Commission, which is without any legal basis," External Affairs Ministry spokesman Randhir Jaiswal said on the Pakistan-China Boundary Joint Commission.
The entire Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh "have been, are and will always remain integral and inalienable parts of India", he said.
"We have never recognised the so-called 'China-Pakistan Boundary Agreement' of 1963 and have consistently maintained that it is illegal and invalid," Mr. Jaiswal said.
The spokesperson added: "We resolutely oppose and reject any attempts to alter the status of these occupied territories or legitimise illegal occupation, impinging on India's sovereignty and territorial integrity." "Any so-called boundary cooperation between China and Pakistan concerning Indian territories would be completely unacceptable and would have no bearing whatsoever on India's sovereignty over these territories," he said.
"Instead of engaging in such theatrics, we call on Pakistan to immediately vacate areas under its illegal and forcible occupation," Mr. Jaiswal said.

stories.headline: Delhi HC seeks Centre view on social media's addictive design
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Delhi high court
 on Wednesday asked the Centre to clarify if it was contemplating a policy to regulate addiction-causing design features on social media platforms like infinite scroll and autoplay.
The court said it would hear after three weeks a PIL seeking constitution of an expert committee to examine engagement-maximising and addiction-causing design features on social media platforms.
On being asked by HC if the Centre was thinking of framing a policy on the issue, ASG Chetan Sharma said he did not have specific instructions on this.
"You take instructions...and we will have the matter after three weeks." During the hearing, Centre and certain social media platforms objected to maintainability of the petition in view of orders of SC and HCs which refused to entertain petitions on a similar issue.
Petitioner Vikas Kathuria said issue is not what content platforms carry, but how they are designed to cause addiction through infinite scroll, autoplay, personalised feeds, notification systems and "likes".

briefs.headline: ICE agent charged with assault, lying about shooting, arrested in Minnesota
briefs.deck: But a lawyer for the ICE agent, Rolando Cantu, said ‌in an interview that his client always intended to answer the charges in Minneapolis.
briefs.bodyText:
A federal immigration officer wanted on assault charges for shooting and wounding a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis was arrested on Wednesday (September 16, 2026), eight months after a confrontation that became a flashpoint over U.S. President Donald Trump’s deportation sweeps.
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro turned himself in to agents of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension in downtown Minneapolis and was booked into the Hennepin County jail on his outstanding arrest warrant, the agency said.
But a lawyer for the ICE agent, Rolando Cantu, said in an interview that his client always intended to answer the charges in Minneapolis. He disputed Hennepin County prosecutors’ assertions that Castro might flee to Mexico, saying, “He wants his day in court.”
Mr. Castro had been released on bond from federal custody earlier this month, wearing a GPS ankle monitor, after an initial appearance in U.S. District Court in McAllen, Texas, on charges of lying to investigators about the circumstances of the January 14 shooting.
The federal indictment charging him with making false statements marked the first U.S. Justice Department prosecution of a federal law enforcement officer accused of wrongdoing arising from the massive Minneapolis ICE deployment dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
Case Stems from operation metro surge
That operation, part of President Donald Trump’s wider immigration crackdown, drew weeks of protests and clashes between ICE and demonstrators, leading to the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal agents.
Mr. Castro already faced state assault charges in Minnesota stemming from the confrontation in which he shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, a Venezuelan national, in the leg through the door of the man’s apartment while children were present inside the home.
The state charges also include false reporting of a crime after Castro allegedly told superiors at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security that Sosa-Celis and others attacked him with a snow shovel and broom, which was disproved by video evidence.
Initial efforts to arrest Mr. Castro were thwarted when the ICE agent returned to his home state of Texas, leading Minnesota officials to issue a warrant for his arrest.
Mr. Castro was apprehended by Texas Rangers, but Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and supporter of Trump’s mass deportation sweeps, refused to sign extradition papers sent by Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat.
Mr. Abbott questioned whether Mr. Castro could be considered a fugitive from justice, and thus subject to extradition, because DHS had reassigned him to his home state of Texas after the Minneapolis shooting.
The ICE agent ultimately spent 90 days in a Texas county jail and was released on August 27 after a federal judge in Texas denied a request from Minnesota to immediately order his extradition. Castro, who Minnesota officials branded a flight risk. He was re-arrested in Texas following his federal grand jury indictment in early September.
DHS has suspended Mr. Castro from ICE, and a person familiar with the case has said a civil rights investigation into the Sosa-Celis shooting had been opened.
Mr. Castro was expected to make his first state court appearance in Minneapolis on Thursday. He will then make an initial appearance in U.S. District Court in neighbouring St. Paul, the state capital, on Friday morning to face charges in the federal indictment.
“Governor Abbott’s attempt to shield Mr. Castro from accountability has failed. We look forward to commencing our prosecution,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who brought the state case, said in a statement.

briefs.headline: Good El Nino? How a bad monsoon left city drenched
briefs.deck: Depression cheer, P 4
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The capital defied the odds this monsoon. As of Sept 16, Delhi had a season's rainfall surplus of 8% in a meteorological subdivision (Haryana) that's reeling under a 23% deficit and a region (northwest India) that has logged a 10% shortfall. The season's peculiar rainfall pattern indicates that a strengthening El Nino as well as climate change may have played a role in giving the capital an unlikely monsoon bounty.
A look at the season's district-level rainfall map of the region shows Delhi literally at the edge of the good monsoon zone this year (see graphic). Just north of the capital lies a swathe of deficient districts starting with neighbouring Sonipat (-32%) and Rohtak (-47%) and all the way up to Hoshiarpur (-53%) and Kapurthala (-69%) in Punjab - a cluster of over 30 rain-starved districts in Haryana and Punjab as well as adjoining Rajasthan, Himachal and west UP.
So how did Delhi turn into a wet pocket next to a rain-deficient region? The answer lies in the way low-pressure systems coming from Bay of Bengal shifted direction this season, probably under the influence of El Nino, and how their interactions with westerly disturbances uniquely aided rains in Delhi-NCR.
Wet capital
A majority of monsoon rainfall in northwest and central India happens under the influence of moisture-laden low-pressure systems (LPSs), including depressions, travelling inland from Bay of Bengal. 
Contrary to what one would expect, the number of such systems does not decrease in an El Nino year. In fact, a 2024 study in Climate Dynamics showed that the number of Bay of Bengal depressions increased in El Nino years in the 1979-2020 period, averaging 3.9 during July-Aug versus 2.4 in normal years.
This year there were 10 LPSs, including four depressions in July-Aug, against a normal of less than nine.
What generally changes in an El Nino year is the direction of the LPSs. "In El Nino years, there is subsidence of air over south India and its adjoining northern parts. This prevents formation of LPSs in the southern latitudes, say in central Bay of Bengal, which would normally move towards the north Andhra-south Odisha coast," said IMD director general Mrutyunjay Mohapatra.
Here's where Delhi benefited, particularly in Aug, when as many as six LPSs, including two depressions, impacted India. With a northward shift, most of these systems entered inland over north Odisha-Bengal and tracked north-northwest, affecting Odisha, Bengal, Jharkhand, UP, Uttarakhand and the Delhi region, with lesser impact in Rajasthan, Haryana and Punjab.
Share your thoughts in the comments

There was another factor in play, likely linked to climate change. WDs are moist wind systems moving east from the Mediterranean region that usually bring wet weather to north India in winter through early summer. Historically, WDs are rare during the monsoons as the jet stream, which causes the disturbance, typically migrates north of the Himalayas by April-May. However, in recent years, the jet stream has persistently been retreating late, a trend scientists attribute to global warming. This year, there were 16 WDs in the June-Aug period - eight in Aug alone, as per IMD.
There were several instances of the easterly monsoon system interacting with a WD, intensifying rainfall over parts of north India, including Delhi. For instance, monsoon's onset over the capital on July 2 happened during an active WD spell. The heaviest rain spells in Delhi (July 8-9, July 29, Aug 7-8, Aug 25) occurred when both a monsoon system and a WD were simultaneously active in the region. These interactions also brought heavy rains in west UP and left a catastrophic footprint in the hills - the Bandipora (J&K) cloudburst, fatal flash floods in Chamba (HP) and forced closure of around 290 roads across HP and Uttarakhand - but don't appear to have majorly impacted Haryana and Punjab.

briefs.headline: Football on table, wrestling without groundwork: Unusual sports India will play at Asiad
briefs.deck: The Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games will introduce Indian spectators to a range of unique sports, such as teqball, kurash, soft tennis, sepak takraw, and sport climbing. These events not only highlight athletic prowess but also celebrate Asian culture. With a delegation of 503 athletes, India will participate robustly, showcasing diverse sporting talents on an international scale.
briefs.bodyText:
The Asian Games have always been more than a showcase of the sports that dominate television screens.
From cricket and hockey to athletics, shooting, badminton and wrestling, some disciplines have a deep following in India. But Aichi-Nagoya 2026 will also put the spotlight on sports that remain largely unfamiliar to the country's mainstream sporting audience.
The 20th edition of the Asian Games will be held in Japan from September 19 to October 4, with around 11,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions competing across 43 sports. India will be represented by 503 athletes across a wide range of disciplines.
Some of those sports are familiar internationally but still developing a following in India. Mixed martial arts, surfing, esports and padel, for instance, are expanding rapidly and have attracted growing global attention.
Then there are sports such as Teqball, Kurash, Soft Tennis, Sepak Takraw and Sport Climbing.
They may not yet command the same audience as cricket, badminton or hockey in India, but they will be part of the country's Asian Games campaign in Japan.
So, what exactly are these sports?
Teqball (Getty Images)
Teqball: When football meets table tennis
If football and table tennis were combined into one sport, the result might look something like Teqball.
Played on a specially designed curved table, Teqball requires players to control and return a football using body parts other than the hands and arms. The sport combines football technique with the precision and rhythm associated with table tennis. Players can compete in singles or doubles, with a maximum of three touches before the ball has to be returned.
The sport was developed in Hungary and has grown rapidly over the past decade.
And Aichi-Nagoya will mark an important milestone: Teqball is making its Asian Games debut as a medal sport. The Olympic Council of Asia added it to the 2026 programme in March.
India will have three representatives:
 Mohamed Anas Imran Beg, Declan Marshall Gonsalves and Quimcy Dsouza. They will compete in men's doubles, mixed doubles and women's singles.
A football becomes the object of a game that looks part tennis rally, part freestyle football and part table-tennis exchange.
Kurash: The wrestling sport where the fight stays on its feet
Kurash may look familiar to anyone who has watched judo or wrestling, but its rules create a distinctly different contest.
An ancient jacket-wrestling tradition from Central Asia, particularly associated with Uzbekistan, Kurash is built around throws rather than ground fighting.
The defining feature is simple: the contest remains standing.
Competitors wear jackets and belts and attempt to throw their opponent onto the back. Groundwork is not permitted, while techniques such as striking, kicking, choking and joint locks are prohibited.
That makes Kurash a fast and explosive sport. There is little of the prolonged ground grappling that audiences might associate with some other combat disciplines. The emphasis is on grip, balance, timing, strength and the ability to execute a clean throw.
Kurash has been part of the Asian Games programme in recent editions, and India already has a small but significant history in the sport.
India won two Kurash medals at the 2018 Asian Games in Jakarta-Palembang, both in the women's 52kg category. Pincky Balhara won silver and Malaprabha Jadhav took bronze.
India's Aichi-Nagoya squad
 includes Vipin Kumar in men's -66kg, Vishal and Yash Kumar in men's +90kg, Bharti and Sangita Balhara in women's -57kg, and Pincky Chauhan in women's -78kg.
For Indian viewers accustomed to wrestling, judo and kabaddi, Kurash is perhaps one of the easier sports to understand once the central rule is known: get the opponent off balance, throw them cleanly and stay on your feet.
Soft Tennis: It looks like tennis, but the ball changes everything
At first glance, Soft Tennis can be mistaken for ordinary tennis.
The court and net are broadly familiar. The players use rackets. The objective is still to hit the ball into the opponent's court.
But the equipment and playing characteristics are different.
Soft Tennis uses a lightweight, air-filled rubber ball rather than the heavier felt-covered ball used in conventional tennis. According to the International Soft Tennis Federation, the ball weighs between 30 and 31 grams. That softer, lighter ball changes the rhythm of the game.
Soft Tennis originated in Japan in the late 19th century and subsequently spread across Asia. It has been part of the Asian Games programme since 1994.
The scoring system is also different from conventional tennis. Rather than the familiar 15-30-40 sequence, Soft Tennis uses numerical scoring, making the scoring easier to follow for newcomers.
India has competed in Soft Tennis at previous Asian Games but is yet to win a medal. Aichi-Nagoya will therefore provide another opportunity to break that drought.
India's six-member squad
 comprises Yogesh Choudhary, Om Yadav, Jay Meena, Aniket Chirag Patel, Aryan Thakur and Aadhya Tiwari. They will compete across the men's team event, men's singles and mixed doubles, with Aadhya also entered in women's singles.
Sepak Takraw
Sepak Takraw: Football skills on a volleyball court
Few Asian sports can produce moments as spectacular as Sepak Takraw.
The sport combines elements of volleyball with the kicking, heading and acrobatic skills associated with football.
Two teams compete across a net, with three players forming a regu. The court is similar in dimensions to a badminton court, while the players are not allowed to use their hands or arms.Feet, knees, chest and head become the main tools.
Each side has a maximum of three touches to control the ball and send it back over the net. The attacking player can then launch into spectacular aerial movements — including scissor kicks and bicycle-kick-style strikes — to send the ball beyond the defence.
The result is one of the most visually striking sports on the Asian Games programme.
Sepak Takraw has been part of the Asian Games since 1990, but it remains relatively unfamiliar to large sections of the Indian sporting audience.
India, however, has been gradually building a record in the discipline.
The country has won two Asian Games bronze medals so far: a men's Team Regu bronze at Jakarta-Palembang 2018 and a women's Regu bronze at Hangzhou 2022.
India will field both men's and women's teams in Aichi-Nagoya, with the men's squad competing in Team Regu and Quadrant events.
The men's contingent
 includes Arun, Jasvir, Ashish Chundawat, Shyam Singh, Lokhon Singh Elangbam, Bobby Kumar, Ashok Singh Mayengbam, Ram Kumar Sharma, O Amarjit Singha, Malemnganba Singh Sorokhaibam, Henary Singh Wahengbam and Akash Yumnam.
The women's contingent
 includes players such as Leirentonbi Devi Elangbam, Prity Langoljam, Menenu Tsukru, Maipak Devi Ayekpam, Priya Devi Elangbam, Shilpa Elangbam, Chaoba Devi Oinam, Seyiekhrieno Tepa and Malemnganbi Yumnam.
For India, Sepak Takraw is no longer an entirely new experiment. The medals in the last two editions have already provided a foundation.
Sport Climbing (Getty Images)
Sport Climbing: Speed, strength and a race against gravity
Sport Climbing may be the most visually recognisable of the five to younger audiences, thanks in part to its growing international profile.
At the Asian Games, climbers compete on artificial walls, using strength, balance, flexibility, technique and problem-solving ability to navigate routes covered with coloured holds.
There are three disciplines: Speed, Boulder and Lead.
Speed is exactly what it sounds like. Climbers race side-by-side up an identical 15-metre wall, with the fastest time deciding the winner.
Boulder is different. Climbers tackle shorter, difficult routes without ropes, relying on technique and problem-solving to complete the designated problems.
Lead takes the contest higher. Climbers attempt to ascend a wall more than 12 metres high, with the result determined by how high they manage to climb within the allotted time.
The three disciplines test different qualities. Speed is about explosive acceleration and precision. Boulder is about solving a physical puzzle. Lead combines endurance, strength and route-reading.
Sport Climbing made its Asian Games debut at Jakarta-Palembang 2018. India has competed in the sport at the last two editions but is yet to win an Asian Games medal.
At Aichi-Nagoya, India's representatives
 include Deepu Mallesh in men's speed and Joga Purty in women's speed.
More than just unfamiliar names
The five sports represent different sides of the Asian Games.
Teqball is a young hybrid sport trying to establish itself on the global stage. Kurash carries centuries of Central Asian tradition into a modern competitive format. Soft Tennis demonstrates how a familiar sport can develop a distinct identity through different equipment and rules. Sepak Takraw showcases Southeast Asia's spectacular athletic culture. Sport Climbing brings strength, speed and problem-solving together on a vertical stage.
They also underline why the Asian Games remain different from the Olympics.
The continental Games have traditionally provided space for sports rooted in particular regions as well as newer disciplines seeking wider international recognition. Aichi-Nagoya's programme includes 43 sports, with Teqball among the new additions and established Asian disciplines such as Kurash, Sepak Takraw and Soft Tennis continuing to feature.
For Indian fans, that means the next few weeks will offer more than the familiar medal races.
There will be moments when a curved table, a jacket throw, a soft rubber ball, an airborne kick or a climber racing up a wall suddenly becomes the centre of attention.

briefs.headline: Devotees gather for historic consecration of Meenakshi temple in Madurai
briefs.deck: Minister Nirmal Kumar expresses pride in elaborate arrangements for the temple consecration ceremony
briefs.bodyText:
As poojas for the consecration ceremony of the Sri Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple are set to begin shortly, the devotees holding permit passes arrived in large numbers at the temple premises.
Expressing pride as final preparations wrapped up, Tamil Nadu Minister for Energy Resources and Law C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar stated that hosting the historic consecration of the Madurai Meenakshi Sundareswarar Temple under the current administration was a matter of profound joy.
“Whatever festival takes place in Madurai is always special. Every arrangement has been meticulously executed under the direct orders of Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, who has personally reviewed the progress of the consecration works over the past three weeks,” Mr. Kumar said while inspecting the final arrangements just hours before the sacred ceremony.
To ensure safety and convenience for the large influx of devotees, authorities have arranged uninterrupted drinking water and electricity supplies, along with robust alternative contingency plans. Fully equipped medical units and ambulances have also been stationed on standby, he noted.
To manage the crowds, a filtering system based on pass colours—red, yellow, purple, and green—is in place, directing devotees to specific access areas closest to the temple core.
Devotees without passes are being categorised as general attendees and will be permitted entry after the official ceremony concludes at 10 a.m.
As announced earlier, drinking water and toilet facilities have been set up at regular intervals throughout the area to assist the public and police personnel. Meanwhile, the special cordon designated for VIPs, judges, and officials has been active since 3 a.m.
Many devotees noted that simply hearing the direct hymns from the temple would suffice, while receiving blessings through the holy water sprayed from atop the temple would make the experience even more meaningful.
“The happiness of the people and all devotees is our true happiness,” he said, emphasising that the primary focus of the government remains the smooth and successful completion of the grand ceremony.
Devotees can enter the temple from the west and south towers and exit through the east tower. For any information, the public can also reach out through toll-free numbers 1800-425-6781 and 1800-425-6782, said a spokesman from the Madurai district administration.
Published - September 17, 2026 06:30 am IST

briefs.headline: Mumbai Police seek clarification from Manoj Jarange over 'contradictory' statements on proposed protest
briefs.deck: The move comes after the police repeatedly denied permission to Jarange for staging a demonstration at Azad Maidan in south Mumbai.
briefs.bodyText:
The Mumbai Police have issued a notice to fasting Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange, seeking clarification on "contradictions" in his statements about his proposed protest in the State capital, officials said on Wednesday (September 16, 2026).
The move comes after the police repeatedly denied Mr. Jarange permission to stage a demonstration at Azad Maidan in South Mumbai.
Officials said Mr. Jarange had initially submitted a letter stating that he would protest alone, accompanied by only 50 people. However, officials said a large crowd of supporters was seen accompanying him as he set off for Mumbai from Jalna district on Tuesday (September 16, 2026).
Also Read | Maratha quota stir: Jarange Patil leaves for Mumbai as police deny nod for protest
In the notice dated September 15, the police asked Mr. Jarange to provide detailed information about the planned demonstration, including the list of volunteers, the total number of people attending, and details of the vehicles being used.
Police said Mr. Jarange's formal undertaking and his public statements are contradictory.
While informing authorities he would protest alone, the activist reportedly appealed to the Maratha community through the media to keep their bags packed and be ready to move to Mumbai upon his call to defend the quota.
Mr. Jarange on Wednesday (September 16) evening said he would stay at Potoda in Beed district for medical treatment and resume his journey to Mumbai to stage an agitation on Thursday (September 17) afternoon.
If anyone stopped him on the way, members of the Maratha community should set out for Maharashtra's capital, he said.
Mr. Jarange, whose hunger strike for reservation demands has entered the 19th day, reached Patoda in the early hours of Wednesday (September 16) and halted in the town as doctors advised him of immediate treatment due to severe dehydration and other health complications.
Published - September 17, 2026 06:33 am IST

briefs.headline: Government functionary questions Rahul's criticism of UPI charges, says Congress MPs in panel gave nod
briefs.deck: Why is Rahul Gandhi opposing something his own MPs, including former finance minister P.Chidambaram and former minister in the UPA government Manish Tewari supported within the parliamentary panel, says a senior government functionary
briefs.bodyText:
The government on Wednesday (September 16, 2026) questioned the rationale behind Congress leader Rahul Gandhi's criticism of the decision to levy a fee on UPI payments to merchants above ₹2,000, saying a parliamentary standing committee had backed such a move and Congress members of the panel had supported it.
A senior government functionary said the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance had pressed for a tiered Merchant Discount Rate (MDR)/ revenue framework for Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and noted that it should be notified and operationalised without delay.
Also Read | Opposition MPs raise concerns over proposed UPI merchant payment fee
Five Congress MPs including P Chidambaram, Manish Tewari, Gaurav Gogoi, Kishori Lal and K Gopinath were present on August 12 when the report was adopted, with no dissent recorded in the published minutes, the functionary said.
"Why is Rahul Gandhi opposing something his own MPs, including former finance minister P.Chidambaram and former minister in the UPA government Manish Tewari supported within the parliamentary panel," the functionary asked.
Reacting to the government's decision to levy a fee on UPI payments above ₹2,000 to merchants, Mr. Gandhi alleged that Prime Minister Narendra Modi has decided to "prostrate" before U.S. President Donald Trump and give a huge amount of money to America.
The Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha also demanded a rollback of the government's decision to levy a fee on UPI payments.
According to the report of the standing committee headed by BJP MP Bhartruhari Mahtab, the panel noted its earlier recommendation emphasising that due to the imperative of a viable revenue model, legislative-enabling provisions for a tiered MDR structure have been brought forward.
However, the committee remained deeply concerned by the staggering mismatch between the ₹2,000-crore allocation and the industry's estimated operational cost of ₹20,700 crore.
In the view of the committee, while statutory enablement now exists to permit calibrated MDR on high-value transactions, any delay in notifying and operationalising this framework leaves payment service providers heavily dependent on inadequate subsidies, thereby threatening critical investments in cybersecurity, fraud prevention and network infrastructure.
Regarding the incentive scheme for promotion of RuPay debit cards and low-value BHIM-UPI transactions (person-to-merchant), the committee, in its report, had further observed and recommended: "The Committee note the massive ₹2000 crore budgetary allocation for 2026-27 designed to offset ecosystem costs caused by the zero-MDR policy on RuPay and low-value UPI transactions.
"The Committee observe that while UPI is expected to process up to 150 billion transactions per month and add 600 million new users, the current government incentive covers merely 11 per cent of the industry's actual costs and 14 per cent of potential MDR collections, creating a structural funding gap impacting long-term infrastructural investment." The committee recommended that while the proposed three-year multi-year scheme and cashback components are necessary to democratise digital payments in untapped Tier 3-6 cities, the Department of Financial Services must concurrently explore a self-reliant, tiered revenue model.
The committee would like to emphasise that establishing a viable revenue mechanism is critical to ensuring that the UPI ecosystem achieves financial sustainability without perpetually straining the government exchequer, it said.
Published - September 17, 2026 06:24 am IST

stories.headline: UPI charge plan draws flak from Bengaluru businesses
stories.deck: In Bengaluru, local merchants are rallying against a suggested MDR affecting UPI payments above Rs 2,000. The imminent implementation of a Rs 5 fee for each such transaction has sent ripples of concern among fuel dealers, pharmacies, and restaurants, who worry it could erode their profits. In response, petroleum dealers have approached the central government, seeking a reprieve from this added…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: The proposed merchant discount rate (MDR) on certain 
UPI
 transactions above Rs 2,000 has drawn opposition from fuel dealers, pharmacies, restaurants and wholesale traders in Bengaluru.
They fear the additional cost could squeeze already thin margins and discourage digital payments.
Come Oct 15, an MDR of Rs 5 will be levied on each UPI transaction above Rs 2,000.
Fuel bunk owners in the city have urged the Centre to exempt petroleum dealers from the proposed MDR.

stories.headline: Bengaluru police to seek legal opinion on complaint against Hariprasad
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 City police will seek legal opinion before considering an investigation into the complaint against 
BK Hariprasad
, president of Karnataka Pradesh Congress Committee (KPCC), for terming imprisoned activist Umar Khalid a “nationalist”.
Hariprasad, also a member of the legislative council, told the media Tuesday that opposition parties and 
ABVP
 had no moral right to speak on Khalid, “who is a nationalist”. A former student researcher, Khalid has been in prison without trial since Sept 2020 after 
Delhi police
 arrested him for his alleged role in planning and executing communal riots.
Condemning Hariprasad for his comments, city-based activist Tejas Gowda filed the complaint with Vidhana Soudha police station Wednesday.

stories.headline: Bengaluru’s infrastructure woes strike a musical chord
stories.deck: The song demands a basic for a city that the Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar says is being viewed internationally: a road that can simply be driven on.
stories.bodyText:
After exhausting all options, a Bengaluru commuter has now turned to artificial intelligence (AI) to generate a song titled Tax Me to request the government to build decent road infrastructure in the city.
The song about Bengaluru’s road infrastructure takes a tongue-in-cheek swipe at the city’s traffic, potholes, flooding, construction, and the endless digging of its roads. The song demands a basic for a city that the Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar says is being viewed internationally: a road that can simply be driven on.
Daily experience to song
Punit Vara, a 34-year-old techie residing near Choodasandra, who uploaded the song on YouTube, said that the song, including its lyrics, was completely AI-generated. It features Doddamara Road, which falls under the Anekal Assembly constituency, represented by A. Shivanna.
“For the past nine months, I drove my pregnant wife on Doddamara Road, which is in a pathetic condition, for regular doctor visits. I had to be extra careful, and it was highly dangerous, which prompted me to come up with this song,” he said. “Besides, I also drive on this road everday,” he added. Mr. Vara said he used his daily experiences of travelling on the road as prompts for generative AI, which came up with the lyrics. He later used another AI model to generate the song using the lyrics, he said.
Mr. Vara terms the song a satire anthem dedicated to every techie, parent, auto driver and commuter surviving Bengaluru’s “moonscape streets” every single day.
Potholes, traffic, construction
For many Bengalureans, the morning commute begins with a familiar ritual, which starts with checking the map, looking at the estimated travel time, and then adding a generous margin for the traffic that the maps could not possibly have accounted for. Now, that daily frustration has found a soundtrack.
“Pothole number 27,” a lyric in the song, takes a dig at the pathetic condition of Doddamara Road in the southeastern outskirts of Bengaluru, which is not very different from the other city roads.
“I pay my income tax. I pay my GST,” the song says, before listing the many other charges that accompany everyday life. The complaint, the song says, is not about wanting “gold-plated roads” or a perfect city. It is about basic infrastructure, including roads without potholes, sidewalks that can be walked on, buses that actually arrive, and streets that do not disappear under water during the monsoon.
Capturing the experience of navigating city’s roads with multiple projects on, the song says: “Metro above me. Digging below, flyover beside me. Nobody knows where to go.” The line captures the geography of a city, where construction seems endless.

stories.headline: Minister asks gram panchayats around Bengaluru to prioritise long-term solution to drinking water woes
stories.bodyText:
Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda on Wednesday chaired the Karnataka Development Programme (KDP) review meeting of the Bengaluru Urban district and directed officials to ensure that gram panchayats fully utilise funds to address drinking water shortage in rural areas of the district. He directed officials to focus on permanent infrastructure instead of temporary measures.
Speaking at the first-quarter KDP review meeting for 2026-27, Mr. Gowda said drinking water should be treated as a basic infrastructure requirement. He asked officials to explore reusing connections of defunct borewells instead of routinely drilling new ones. “Several proposals are being received seeking funds to drill new borewells. There are more than 1,000 borewells that have remained defunct for years. The RR numbers of these inactive borewells should be transferred to new connections wherever feasible,” he said.
Mr. Gowda directed officials to complete the exercise before the next review meeting. He said a portion of gram panchayat grants should be earmarked for durable infrastructure, particularly drinking water, and waste management. “Development cannot be measured merely by how much money has been spent. Every rupee spent must translate into a solution to a problem faced by people,” he said.
He expressed concern over waste management in rural areas and said a more scientific approach was required to address the issue.
The Minister said scope for new roads had been identified in the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region Development Authority (BMRDA) limits around Bengaluru following an exercise undertaken over the past year. Some existing roads would also be widened, he said, warning that strict action would be taken against officials if negligence or rule violations were found in implementing the projects.
He further directed officials to identify vacant sites under gram panchayat jurisdiction for developing parks, playgrounds, and sports facilities. Such land should be formally handed over for the purpose, with compound walls constructed on priority, followed by development of the facilities based on fund availability.

briefs.headline: 18-year-old dies of electrocution during Ganesha immersion in Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
Kolar:
 An 18-year-old student died of electrocution while removing decorative lighting installed near a Ganesha pandal at Beerandahalli village in Bangarapet taluk Wednesday.
The deceased has been identified as Mithun, a resident of Beerandahalli. He was a II PU student at a private college in Kolar. According to locals, the incident took place when Mithun was removing the decorative lights at the pandal ahead of Ganesha immersion. He accidentally came in contact with a live wire near the site and collapsed.
Villagers rushed to his aid and provided first aid before shifting him to a hospital in a car. However, doctors declared him brought dead. A woman who witnessed the incident is said to have told police that a water pipe and other materials were lying close to the electrical wires and might have triggered the tragedy.
Ravikumar, police inspector of Bangarapet, said the incident occurred around 8.30am Wednesday. According to him, while villagers were celebrating the festival together under a common pandal, Mithun and his father had chosen to celebrate separately.
The idol had been donated to them by some individuals and was installed near the village temple. They had drawn power from the temple for the decorative lighting around the idol. 
The villagers had reportedly advised them to join the common celebrations.
DSP Lakshmaiah visited the spot and inspected the electrical connections and decorative lighting arrangements. Police are investigating the circumstances that led to the electrocution, including the status of the power connection and whether adequate safety measures had been followed.

briefs.headline: From glass floors to cafes, Rs 600-crore Bengaluru skydeck may offer views and thrills
briefs.deck: BDA floats tender for advisory service
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 The state govt’s proposed 250-metre-high skydeck is being envisioned as much more than a towering viewing structure, with govt now exploring a broader mix of tourism, entertainment, leisure and commercial attractions. But even as the project gathers fresh momentum, questions over its execution, financial structure and the eventual form of the ambitious landmark remain.
The project could feature panoramic viewing decks, elevated walkways, glass-bottom viewing areas, experience centres, restaurants and cafés, retail outlets, entertainment facilities and digital immersive zones. The final mix of attractions, however, is yet to be decided and is expected to depend on the site’s development potential, market demand and financial viability.
Bangalore Development Authority (BDA) has now floated a tender to appoint a transaction adviser to take the project forward under a public-private partnership (PPP) model. The tentative project cost has been pegged at around Rs 600 crore. The appointment of a transaction adviser is expected to provide greater clarity on how the project will actually be executed. The adviser will assess the technical, commercial and financial feasibility of the project and recommend an appropriate PPP structure, investment model and revenue-sharing mechanism, besides identifying potential revenue streams.
The skydeck has been among the state govt’s ambitious plans for the city. Earlier this year, the govt identified nearly 45 acres at Bheemanakuppe-Challaghatta in Nadaprabhu Kempegowda Layout in western Bengaluru for the project. The site is located close to the Bengaluru-Mysuru access-controlled highway and has connectivity to Bengaluru-Mysuru Highway and Magadi Road.
Before settling on the present site, the authorities had examined at least six locations for the proposed skydeck. The repeated evaluation of sites had added to uncertainty over where the structure would eventually come up, while questions also remained over the scale of investment required and the commercial model needed to sustain the project.
The transaction adviser will now undertake a detailed assessment of the selected site and determine whether it can support the proposed structure and associated attractions. The study will examine road, Metro and public transport connectivity, surrounding infrastructure, expected visitor footfall, tourism potential and the visibility of the location.
It will also evaluate parking requirements, utilities, land-use compatibility, visitor movement, environmental considerations and safety requirements — all crucial factors for a structure expected to attract large crowds.
The adviser will study market demand, site potential and commercial opportunities before advising BDA on the project’s financial viability and implementation framework. The exercise is also expected to determine how much private investment can be mobilised and what revenue-generating facilities can be incorporated into the development.
The latest vision marks a shift from the initial perception of the skydeck as simply a 250-metre observation tower. By combining viewing facilities with entertainment, hospitality, retail and immersive experiences, the govt hopes to create a destination capable of generating sustained visitor footfall and revenue.
What the project may promise
-Sky observation deck
-Elevated walkways
-Glass-bottom viewing zones, where technically feasible
-Experience centres
-Restaurants and cafés
-Souvenir and shopping outlets
-Recreational and entertainment facilities
-Immersive and interactive experiences
-Exhibition and event spaces

briefs.headline: Locals attack family over alleged kidnap in Bengaluru, 6 injured
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: High drama unfolded on Magadi Road Wednesday night after a group of locals allegedly thrashed several men and damaged their car, suspecting they were trying to kidnap a young woman. Six persons, including a nine-year-old girl, sustained injuries in the commotion.
However, the alleged kidnapping took a dramatic turn when the woman intervened and told the crowd that the men were her own family members, including her father, who had come from 
Rajasthan
 to take her back home.
Speaking to police who arrived at the spot, the woman said she had married a man from another caste despite her family’s opposition. She alleged that her family had recently traced her to Bengaluru and was trying to force her to return to Rajasthan. “I’ve married a man from another caste and my family was against it. Recently, we came here and my family somehow followed me,” she told police.
A senior police officer said the woman was being requested to lodge a complaint against her family so that action could be taken.
Meanwhile, the family’s vehicle was badly damaged after the crowd attacked it. The family members allegedly tried to flee the spot, ramming into other vehicles in the process, officials added.
Of those injured, one woman with serious head injuries has been shifted to the ICU of a nearby private hospital, police added. Cops said they are yet to register a case. Suspects have been detained and the car used in the “kidnapping” seized, police said.

briefs.headline: No fixing, just listening: Bengaluru’s sharing circles make room for difficult conversations
briefs.bodyText:
On weekend mornings, small circles are forming across Bengaluru, where strangers gather to say the things that are usually left unsaid: the weight of family expectations, the ache of feeling left behind, the fear of ageing and the vulnerability of intimacy. Some truths are easier to share with someone who doesn’t already know your story.
Sharing circles offer a space for such conversations: where people speak from lived experience and are heard, without anyone rushing to fix, advise, or resolve. What do they get in return? The rare gift of being understood without having to explain.
‘There is no expert in this experience’
Unlike a panel discussion, where a subject is often approached through research, professional knowledge or clinical practice, these conversations place lived experience at the centre. “We had panels happening on stage, with panellists talking about a topic from a place of research or clinical practice. But a sharing circle is something that is entirely lived experience. There is no expert in a sharing circle. It is people who share that experience coming together,” says Natasha Joshi, strategy officer of an organising committee.
Participation is voluntary, and listeners are discouraged from interrupting, judging or offering unsolicited solutions. 
Facilitators help ensure that the discussion remains balanced, while participants may recognise their own experiences in someone else’s account. “They also have a space to share how they have experienced something similar,” facilitator Shashanka Lakshmipati says, adding, “When facilitators show vulnerability themselves, it can help participants feel more comfortable opening up.”
‘The space is not solution-oriented’
The purpose of such conversations is not necessarily to arrive at an answer. “Unlike a workshop, which usually works towards a defined outcome, a sharing circle is an exploration around a theme,” says Shashanka. “One of the things that sets a sharing circle apart is that it isn’t solution-oriented. There isn’t really one problem that we’re trying to solve. The idea is to offer a space where emotions and feelings can be explored in a community, and not necessarily to solve the problem,” he adds.
‘These are conversations that are difficult to hold’
The subjects are often familiar, but can be difficult to articulate in everyday settings. “These are conversations that may be experienced by a large number of people, but are difficult to talk about or not very easy to hold,” says Yashasvi Murli, a mental health and gender officer. The discussions cover different stages of life, including young adults dealing with family expectations, people who feel they are falling behind, midlife, ageing, childfree choices, male friendships, intimacy and adoption.
‘We are better together as a community’
This openness to sharing one’s inner life with a group isn’t new at all. It may simply be a return to how people in India have always lived, bound together in community rather than apart. “We are group-based cultures. We exist in groups. We don’t have a highly individuated kind of existence,” says Natasha.
For Shashanka, listening to another person’s experience can offer a sense of recognition without requiring a direct solution. “When people share their experiences, perspectives and thoughts, others can relate and feel, ‘I am not alone’, and that itself can be a powerful experience,” he says.
Yashasvi adds that participants often support one another. “When emotions get unlocked, and people cry or talk about things they have never spoken about out loud, it is often the others with similar experiences who hold that space. They bring in empathy and know what to say in ways that only somebody with that kind of experience can.”

briefs.headline: Double-decker push: BMRCL Board to decide on 37km-to-11km plan
briefs.deck: Sources Say govt ‘agreed’ to build double-decker flyovers at traffic bottlenecks
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The proposal to scale down the double-decker flyover from 37km to 11km will shortly be placed before the Bangalore Metro Rail Corporation Ltd (BMRCL) Board for a final decision, potentially bringing an end to the prolonged uncertainty surrounding the ambitious road-and-Metro project.
Sources said that BMRCL has managed to convince the state govt to reconsider its earlier plan to build an end-to-end double-decker structure along the Namma Metro Phase III corridors. Instead, the corporation is now looking at shorter double-decker stretches at key junctions where traffic congestion is particularly severe.
The move follows recommendations by engineering consultancy RITES, which advised against constructing a continuous double-decker flyover along the entire corridor. RITES suggested that BMRCL should instead focus on specific locations where elevated road infrastructure could help ease major traffic bottlenecks. A technical study by the IISc Sustainable Transportation Lab also raised serious concerns over constructing a double-decker flyover along the proposed Orange Line.
BMRCL had proposed a 37km double-decker structure along Namma Metro’s Phase III Orange Line, with a road flyover at the lower level and the Metro viaduct above. 
The road component was estimated to cost around Rs 9,700 crore, with the state govt agreeing to fund it.
The 45km Phase III project received Centre’s approval in Aug 2024, but BMRCL could not proceed with construction after the state proposed incorporating the double-decker road infrastructure. Chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
, who was then handling Bengaluru’s development portfolio as deputy CM, had backed the proposal, arguing that additional road capacity would help ease congestion.
With the project facing delays, BMRCL commissioned engineering consultancy RITES to examine the feasibility of the double-decker plan. In its report, RITES raised questions over the viability of constructing an end-to-end elevated road alongside the Metro. It cautioned that continuously adding road capacity could encourage greater private-vehicle use and undermine the Metro’s objective of shifting commuters to public transport.
The consultancy also flagged engineering complications, noting that the combined structure could rise to nearly 35 metres at some locations to cross existing flyovers and Metro corridors. Financial viability was another concern: while the Metro-only project has an estimated economic internal rate of return (EIRR) of around 17%, the figure falls below the 14% benchmark when the double-decker component is included.
BMRCL is now considering a shorter, targeted approach, with double-decker structures proposed only at major traffic bottlenecks. Possible locations include Hebbal, BEL Circle, Goraguntepalya, Sumanahalli Cross, Nagarbhavi, Nayandahalli, Kamakya Junction, Sarakki Junction, Delmia flyover and Vega City Mall.
When the project was initially proposed, road-cum-Metro flyovers were planned only at two locations — one to ease traffic congestion at Sarakki Junction, over the existing Green Line, for a length of 1.4km, and another from Kamakya to Ittamadu-Hoskerehalli for a length of 1.5km.

briefs.headline: Karnataka State Pollution Control Board bats for carpooling to curb vehicular emissions in Bengaluru
briefs.deck: The KSPCB said that their Source Apportionment Study conducted for Bengaluru under the National Clean Air Programme found that vehicular emissions contributed nearly 40% of the overall Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5 load, making them the single largest contributor to PM2.5 pollution.
briefs.bodyText:
After the Bengaluru Traffic Police (BTP), the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB) has now urged the Transport Department to examine the feasibility of introducing a clear regulatory framework for non-commercial shared commuting and corporate carpooling initiatives in Bengaluru.
The letter, written by R. Gokul, member secretary of KSPCB, addressed to the commissioner of the Transport Department, cited the potential of such measures to reduce vehicular emissions and congestion in the city.
The letter comes in the backdrop of KSPCB, under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), implementing various measures to improve air quality in Bengaluru.
Large vehicular emissions
The KSPCB said that their Source Apportionment Study conducted for Bengaluru under the National Clean Air Programme (NCAP) found that vehicular emissions contributed nearly 40% of the overall Particulate Matter (PM) 2.5 load, making them the single largest contributor to PM2.5 pollution. Meanwhile, road dust contributed approximately 51% of PM10 concentrations.
The Board said the increasing number of private vehicles, coupled with severe congestion on major corridors and junctions, was leading to higher emissions of particulate matter and gaseous pollutants. “Slow-moving traffic and inefficient vehicle movement also contributed to the resuspension of road dust, aggravating ambient air pollution levels,” the board noted.
Stakeholders’ meeting
Mr. Gokul told The Hindu that vehicular emissions continued to be a major source of air pollution in the city. To address the issue, they were exploring options, for which meetings with several stakeholders involved in promoting shared mobility and carpooling solutions in Bengaluru were held.
“In one of the meetings, a stakeholder presented the positive adaptations through which congestion and slow-moving traffic, especially in high-density corridors, can be addressed. Such implementations, which also include carpooling, could curb the emissions, helping the cause of NCAP,” he said.
The discussions majorly highlighted the potential role of organised carpooling platforms in reducing single-occupancy vehicle use, mitigating traffic congestion, reducing fuel consumption, and lowering vehicular emissions, according to Mr. Gokul.
The Hindu earlier reported that the traffic department’s internal audit, based on data gathered from private aggregators, shows that before 2021, nearly 60,000 people benefitted from carpooling. At present, that number has dropped to 25,000. The analysis predicts that more than 1.5 lakh people will use carpooling daily if it is fully legalised and widely publicised.
Regulatory ambiguity
In the letter, the Board acknowledged that regulatory ambiguities remained regarding the operation and promotion of organised carpooling arrangements. The absence of a clearly articulated regulatory framework, it said, could create uncertainty for commuters, employers, technology platforms, and enforcement agencies.
Hence, the KSPCB has sought that the Transport Department, as the competent authority on motor vehicle regulation and passenger transport policy, examine the matter from a policy and regulatory perspective.
It suggested that the department consider issuing guidelines, clarifications, or a policy framework governing non-commercial shared commuting and corporate carpooling, with safeguards relating to safety, accountability, and compliance with applicable laws.

briefs.headline: Despite curbs, over 4,000 PoP Ganesha idols immersed in Bengaluru
briefs.deck: The Karnataka State Pollution Control Board, in coordination with municipality officials and the police, launched a strict enforcement drive and seized over 3,000 Ganesha idols made of PoP.
briefs.bodyText:
Despite an enforcement effort to curb plaster of Paris (PoP) Ganesha idols this year, the streets of Bengaluru still witnessed thousands of PoP idols being immersed during the two-day immersion period on September 14 and 15.
Data from the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) shows that at least 4,280 PoP idols were immersed across the five city corporations during the two days. This included 3,512 idols on September 14 and 768 on September 15.
The Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB), in coordination with municipality officials and the police, launched a strict enforcement drive and seized over 3,000 Ganesha idols made of PoP. The KSPCB also warned against using immersing Ganesha idols made with PoP idols in lakes, stating that it is a violation of law and is punishable by a penalty and imprisonment ranging from a minimum of one and a half years up to six years.
However, the GBA’s statistics covering immersions at permanent lake locations, temporary artificial tanks and kalyanis, and mobile tanks, show that PoP idols continued to account for a significant number of immersions despite efforts to restrict their use.
On September 14, the West City Corporation recorded the highest number of PoP idol immersions at 1,744, followed by Central with 548, South with 630, East with 424, and North with 167 . On September 15, the West corporation recorded 342, followed by East with 170, Central with 114, South with 132, and North with 10.
In all, Bengaluru recorded the immersion of 1,97,744 Ganesha idols, including earthen ones, across the five city corporations under the GBA on September 14 and 15, according to data compiled by the civic bodies.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru’s Goethe Institut hosts six German artists as part of residency program
briefs.deck: We look at what six artists-in-residence from Germany hope to create during their time in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
This year, Goethe Institut/Max Mueller Bhavan in Bengaluru, welcomed six artists-in-residence from Germany; similarly, artists from Karnataka and Kerala who are a part of the institute’s Bangalore Residency Expanded program will be sent to Germany. Goethe Institut has partnered with the likes of ISRO, Namma Katte, Indian Music Experience and other cultural spaces in the city to host these artists.
“The residency initiative began in 2009,” says Nandita Nirgudkar, head of cultural programmes at the Goethe Institut, “but back then it was individual residencies. Our group residencies started in 2013.”
The artists in residence are new to the city, so their central focus will be on meeting people and learning from them. They will engage with local artistic and cultural spaces, dive into traditions and art practices in the city and look forward to collaborations.
Goethe Institut recently organised Spot On, an event for the residents to introduce themselves, their work and research in Bengaluru.
Animation artist Nikki Schuster is being hosted by Science Gallery and her experimental works and explore the oft-unnoticed aspects of society. The working title for her project here is MICROPOLIS and she says, “I want to work on the micro, little perspectives set in this big metropolis; I also want to focus on methods of food production as it plays a big role in global climate change.”
The Indian Music Experience Museum will host Thomas Lea Clarke, a sound artiste and musician from Berlin. “I am new to India, both sonically and culturally,” says Thomas, whose work revolves around audio technology and how it carries histories. He says “I am going to let my focus be guided by the people I meet and the music that I come across.”
As a sound artiste based in Berlin, Abel Korinsky’s work is interdisciplinary. He sees this residency as “a chance to respectfully learn from people, and to understand how things work. At the same time, I am trying to understand how digital media is shaping our perception.” He also wishes to learn and observe during his time at the Indian Sonic and Research Organisation in the city. His thought experiments look at soundscapes as archives of history and heritage.
Visual artist Christine Koschel says, “I am interested in the everyday moments of life that you ignore,” and this philosophy of hers resides in conceptual artworks using media such as food and cutlery. Her initial plan was to study the protest songs, yet, upon arriving, she says it is possible her work will transcend into something completely different.
Herlambang Bayu Aji hails from Java, Indonesia, and his art revolves around its social issues. Currently based in Berlin, he will be hosted by the National Centre for Biological Sciences. His art mainly focuses on shadow puppetry. Having created over a hundred puppets for his own method of child-friendly storytelling, Bayu is looking forward to learning about Togalu Gombeyaata, the shadow-puppet tradition of Karnataka.
Suresh Jayaram of 1Shantiroad Studio will host Yana Tsegay, an artist from Frankfurt whose research will focus on Lal Bagh Botanical Garden as a cultivated environment. When asked about her work, she says, “Seeing how a city can be shaped by plants and greenery is special to me and I am curious to experience that; besides, there are many geological monuments here that can inspire me.”
The artists-in-residence program will be on till October 31, 2026.
For more details visit https://www.goethe.de/ins/in/en/index.html

stories.headline: NZ parliament gives nod to FTA, rollout likely in Oct
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: New Zealand parliament has voted in favour of the trade agreement with India, setting the stage for its operationalisation. "People told me a FTA with India wasn't possible. Well, today that deal passed its final vote in Parliament. It's happening. National said we'd secure an FTA with India in our first term, and we've delivered. This landmark deal means more jobs, higher incomes for Kiwis. It means more New Zealand products being sold in India by opening the door to 1.4 billion Indian consumers," New Zealand PM Christopher Luxon said in a social media post.
The agreement, expected to be operationalised next month, will allow duty-free access to all exports from India, with New Zealand also committing to invest $20 billion in the country.
Govt will lower tariffs on wine and cut import duty for specified quantities of apples, kiwi and types of honey. India will get easier access for services in NZ, along with easier visa rules for professionals.

stories.headline: After Senate, US House passes Russia sanctions bill; 100% tariff threat looms for India
stories.deck: The US House has successfully passed a sanctions bill aimed at Russian officials and the energy sector. This new legislation empowers President Trump to impose tariffs on significant buyers of Russian oil. India might encounter a staggering 100 percent tariff on its imports due to its energy dealings with Russia. The bill also broadens sanctions against Russia and prolongs measures against Iran…
stories.bodyText:
The US House of Representatives on Wednesday passed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill that targets Russian officials, banks and the country’s energy trade, while giving President Donald Trump the power to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil and gas, including India.
The 'Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026' passed 262-159 and now heads to Trump, who is expected to sign it into law, reported Reuters.
For India, the legislation allows creating a new legal route for Washington to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on Indian imports over New Delhi’s continued purchases of Russian energy. India and China are among the biggest buyers of Russian crude, and the tariff provision is intended in part to put pressure on countries that continue to support Russia’s energy revenues.
The measure directs the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas. It includes an exception for countries that import less than 15 per cent of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those purchases.
What the Russia sanctions bill does
The legislation expands sanctions against Russian officials and financial institutions and targets vessels in Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which has helped keep Russian energy exports moving despite existing Western restrictions.
Its tariff provisions are aimed at using access to the US market as leverage against countries that continue to purchase Russian energy. Supporters have specifically pointed to China and India as major targets of the measure.
The bill is named after the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who spent more than a year negotiating the sanctions package. It also includes measures targeting Iran and extends existing sanctions on the country for five years.
Trump’s backing was important to the legislation’s progress after he had previously criticised efforts to provide further US support to Ukraine. Graham eventually secured Trump’s support after the package incorporated the president’s push for an extension of Iran sanctions.
The legislation comes after Trump has repeatedly criticised countries including India over its purchases of Russian crude and accused New Delhi of helping finance Moscow’s war in Ukraine.
If enacted and subsequently used by Trump, the new authority could give the administration another mechanism to raise the cost of Indian goods entering the US market because of India’s Russian energy purchases.
The bill does not itself impose a 100 per cent tariff on Indian goods. Rather, it gives the US president the authority to impose such tariffs under specified conditions.
Supporters of the provision say the threat is intended to discourage major economies from buying Russian energy and reduce the revenues available to Moscow to finance its war.
“These countries have a choice to make about whether they will continue to sustain Putin's aggression,” said Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas.
Democrats divided over tariff powers
The legislation drew opposition from some Democrats, who supported continued backing for Ukraine but raised concerns about giving Trump broad authority to use tariffs against US allies.
Critics argued that the tariffs could ultimately raise prices for American consumers, while also allowing the administration to target European countries and other US partners.
“This president has always said he loves tariffs,” said Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y. “And we know the history of what he's done with reference to tariffs to our European allies, and our allies everywhere.”
Democratic lawmakers were also divided over whether passing the bill would strengthen US support for Ukraine or give Trump powers that could be used in ways they oppose.
“If we fail to pass this bill, there will be cheers in the Kremlin and tears in Kyiv,” said Rep. Steny Hoyer, D-Md.
Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., meanwhile, warned that supporters of the legislation could later regret backing it if Trump used its tariff and sanctions provisions against US allies.
“Yes they will be able to say ‘we stood with Ukraine’ in the immediate aftermath,” Beyer said. “But when Donald Trump hits our allies with new tariffs and waives sanctions on Russia, the propaganda victory for Putin will be lasting, and the damage will be embedded in U.S. law.”
Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said Democrats would continue to support Ukraine but argued that the legislation did not provide a clear route to securing the country.
Senate had already passed the bill
The Senate approved the legislation by an overwhelming 86-11 vote on August 7, but action subsequently slowed in the House amid disagreements over its tariff provisions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had pushed for congressional approval of the sanctions package and appealed to House lawmakers before Wednesday’s vote.
“During the war, it is sometimes better to make a not-so-perfect decision than to do nothing,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post ahead of the vote.
The House passage marks the most significant congressional action in support of Ukraine since Trump returned to the White House, after lawmakers had struggled to maintain momentum for further US funding and military assistance to Kyiv.
The legislation now goes to Trump for his signature. Once enacted, the administration will have additional sanctions and tariff powers to pressure Russia and countries continuing to trade in Russian energy.

stories.headline: Mining amendment is unfair to States
stories.deck: A State that bears the infrastructural and social consequences of mineral extraction must retain a meaningful stake in the economic value generated from its natural resources
stories.bodyText:
India’s mineral wealth is not evenly spread across the country. States such as Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, and Karnataka possess enormous reserves of coal, iron ore, and other minerals that feed industries across India. While mining brings in investment and employment, it also leaves the host State to deal with challenges such as the resettlement of displaced groups; environmental damage; pressure on public infrastructure; and the long-term consequences of extracting minerals that can never be replaced.
That is why the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act (MMDR), 2026 deserves closer attention. At the heart of the amendment is Section 9D which restricts State Governments from imposing taxes, cesses or other levies on mineral rights or mineral-bearing land except in accordance with conditions prescribed by the Central government. The Centre says the measure is intended to create a predictable tax environment, prevent excessive levies, and to encourage long-term investment in mining. There is an understandable economic argument behind that objective. Mining projects involve enormous investments and operate over decades; investors need to know that the financial rules will not change unpredictably from one year to another. However, this logic has been contested by the States.
The real question is not merely whether States will continue receiving the royalty, the auction premium and other revenues they receive today. The Centre claims that 90% of mining sector revenue accrues to the States and that this will continue. The larger concern is about what States may be prevented from earning tomorrow.
A mineral-rich State possesses a natural economic advantage. Ordinarily, one would expect it to have some ability to use that advantage to raise resources for its own development. Section 9D substantially reduces that freedom by making future State levies related to minerals dependent upon a framework controlled by the Centre. This matters enormously for States whose budgets are closely connected with mining. NITI Aayog’s Fiscal Health Index has highlighted the strong performance of Odisha and Chhattisgarh in mobilising revenue and has specifically recognised the role played by mining receipts. In Odisha, mining has accounted for a large proportion of the State’s non-tax revenue. Mineral producing districts often require greater public expenditure because they bear the costs of mining.
The federal problem
The constitutional issue is equally significant. The Constitution gives States the power to tax mineral rights under Entry 50 of the State List, although Parliament can impose limitations on that power through laws relating to mineral development. States also possess a separate constitutional power to tax lands and buildings under Entry 49 of the State List.
In 2024, a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court in Mineral Area Development Authority vs. Steel Authority of India held, among other things, that royalty payable on minerals is not a tax. It also recognised the States’ legislative power to tax mineral rights and held that mineral-bearing land can fall within the States’ taxation power over land. The 2026 Amendment risks rendering the impact of this judgment nugatory.
While Entry 50 permits Parliament to place limitations upon State taxation on mineral rights, Section 9D of the amending statute goes further by extending its restriction to taxes or levies on mineral-bearing lands. That is likely to raise an important debate: how far can a Central law dealing with mineral development restrict a State’s exclusive power to tax land? The issue is larger than mining policy alone. It concerns the relationship between the Union and the States.
India’s federal system cannot function effectively if States have responsibilities without financial capacity. A State that bears the infrastructural and social consequences of mineral extraction must retain a meaningful stake in the economic value generated from its natural resources. Uniformity may make taxation more predictable, but predictability should not come at the cost of narrowing the fiscal choices available to States.
The debate over the MMDR Amendment should therefore not be reduced to a contest between promoting investment and imposing taxes. The minerals beneath a State’s soil may serve the entire country, but the costs of extracting them are felt most directly by the people who live above them.
Ashok Kumar Panda is a Senior Advocate; Aniruddha Purushotham is an Advocate

stories.headline: What India’s growth really means
stories.deck: India should counter energy risks through diversified suppliers, long term contracts, strategic reserves, renewables, domestic exploration and efficiency
stories.bodyText:
India’s 7.8% real GDP growth in April to June 2026 is an extension of a strong economic journey — real GDP grew 7.2% in 2023-24, 7.1% in 2024-25, and 7.7% in 2025-26. The latest rate exceeds the RBI’s 7% forecast despite the West Asian conflict, high energy prices, and uncertain trade. Its real significance, however, lies in the breadth of production and demand.
Real GDP, which is the value of goods and services after adjusting for inflation, rose to ₹81.36 lakh crore, while real GVA, the value added by farms, factories and services before adjusting for product taxes and subsidies, grew by 8.2% to ₹73.82 lakh crore. Manufacturing rose by 9.2%, utilities 8.9% and construction 7.7%, lifting the secondary sector by 8.6%. Services grew by 10%, led by finance, real estate, IT and professional services at 12.1%. Agriculture grew by 3.6%, although mining contracted by 2.4%. This is broad-based growth with identifiable weak spots.
This strength is reinforced by demand. Gross fixed capital formation grew by 11.9%, private consumption by 7.1% and real exports 12%. Using the same gross fixed capital formation measure for 2023-24, investments by private corporations were 10.3% of GDP. While the general government invested 4.2%, total public sector investment was 7.8% when adding in investments by public corporations. Moreover, when adding in household investments, mainly housing and unincorporated businesses, total non-public investment was 24.1% of GDP. That is, while public capital expenditure has built the platform, the next acceleration requires more private investment.
Fast growing economy
The base year change is simple. A base year removes inflation and reflects the economy’s structure. Updating it from 2011-12 to 2022-23 replaces an outdated market basket with today’s products, services and prices. Some estimates may rise and others fall, but changing the ruler does not shrink the economy. On comparable year-on-year data, India’s 7.8% exceeded Malaysia’s 6%, Singapore’s 5.9%, Indonesia’s 5.29%, and China’s 4.3%.
Editorial | Testing times: On India’s GDP growth data
India is therefore among the fastest growing major economies. Its expanding market supports global demand for energy, technology, machinery and services, while offering a trusted location for diversified supply chains. This advances India’s path to becoming the world’s third largest economy in nominal terms. Since rankings also reflect prices and exchange rates, the milestone will endure only if real growth leads to higher productivity, stronger firms, and better household incomes. Employment is the decisive test. India added 17.19 crore jobs between 2014-15 and 2023-24, according to RBI KLEMS-based data. The next employment revolution must improve job quality through productivity, wages, formalisation, social security and skilling. While women’s labour force participation reached 41.7% in 2023-24, safe transport, affordable childcare, flexible work, credit and market access are essential to bring many more women into productive employment.
Manufacturing must move from assembly to design, components, machinery, electronics and clean technology, while services must spread beyond metros into tourism, health, education, logistics, finance and Indian language digital businesses. AI preparedness must move from adoption to original capability through domestic compute, Indian language data, research talent, and trusted applications. India must also make proper use of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs). An FTA utilisation mission should guide firms on rules of tariffs and markets. MSMEs need hand-holding on non-tariff barriers through shared testing, affordable certification, standards, customs support and buyer discovery. Moreover, external ambition requires domestic resilience. India should counter energy risks through diversified suppliers, long term contracts, strategic reserves, renewables, domestic exploration and efficiency. Timely infrastructure, predictable regulation, easier credit, and stable taxation can crowd in private investment.
The 7.8% quarter warrants confidence, not complacency. India must convert public capital expenditure into private investment, job numbers into quality employment, and FTAs into opportunities for MSMEs. If energy and macroeconomic stability accompany inclusion, productivity, and transparent measurement, becoming the third largest economy will be more than a statistical milestone. It will become a foundation for broad-based prosperity.
Gourav Vallabh is Professor of Finance, XLRI and Part Time Member, Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister. Views are personal
